case_study_insert.main_stem: Juniper Row Collective (JRC) is a cooperative in the ethical fashion retail sector, employing a workforce of 36. Founded in 2011 by Iris Juniper, the business sells fair-trade clothing through a chain of boutiques across five cities and an online shop, and operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. JRC plans to invest $760,000 in a new central distribution hub, financed by a $460,000 ten-year bank loan and $300,000 from the sale of assets. It has fixed costs of $266,000 a year, a variable cost of $20 a unit and a selling price of $34, and currently produces 48,000 units a year. JRC faces two problems: labour turnover is rising and garment return rates have increased.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Quality and Marketing Report, Q3 2025: JRC's boutiques and online shop sold 11,400 garments last quarter with a returns rate of 4.3%, down from 6.2% last year. Customer complaints fell from 33 to 19 per month. Average stock replenishment time is 6.4 days. A survey of 410 shoppers found 66% would pay up to $2.50 more for ethically made clothing, and 58% check labour practices before buying. Records show 11 of 36 staff still need induction on the new stock-control tablets; off-the-job training courses at the local college cost $820 per employee, while on-the-job training is provided in each boutique.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Juniper Row Collective as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 4.5% to 5.25%, raising borrowing costs on variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage rises by 5.8% from $13.40 to $14.18 an hour from April 2026. (3) Wholesale fabric and import costs have risen 10.4% year on year, while spending on ethical fashion grew 4.2%.

questions.question_text: JRC plans to fund part of its distribution hub with a ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for JRC of using the sale of assets to finance the expansion instead of the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Selling assets raises $300,000 immediately without interest or repayment, so JRC avoids adding debt to the $460,000 bank loan already planned. With fixed costs of $266,000 a year and fabric and import costs up 10.4%, preserving cash protects the $34 selling price and the 66% of surveyed shoppers who value ethical clothing.

Point 2: The sale of assets does not dilute the cooperative's ownership or give lenders control, so Iris Juniper and the members keep decision-making over the $760,000 hub. Freeing cash tied up in unused assets also improves liquidity, which matters given the 58% of 410 shoppers who check labour practices before buying and expect JRC to honour its ethical claims.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage of the sale of assets identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to JRC's costs, finance and survey evidence.

questions.question_text: JRC is launching a new ethically made clothing range online. Consider a national television campaign, search-engine advertising, or fashion influencer marketing. Which should JRC choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Television campaign: A national TV advert could raise awareness of JRC's ethical range across all five cities and beyond, but airtime is very expensive for a 36-employee cooperative funding a $760,000 hub. Much of the mass audience would not buy fair-trade clothing online, so the spend would be poorly targeted.

Search-engine advertising: Paid search reaches shoppers looking for ethical fashion and can be capped to a budget, protecting cash alongside the $460,000 loan. Its weakness is that it captures only existing demand and cannot tell the labour-practices story that 58% of 410 shoppers check, while clicks in fashion categories are costly.

Fashion influencer marketing: Ethical-fashion influencers can demonstrate the garments and explain the fair-trade credentials to an audience that already cares, matching the 66% of shoppers who would pay $2.50 more. Engagement is measurable and credibility high, though results depend on the influencer's reputation and can build slowly.

Recommendation: JRC should choose fashion influencer marketing with a small search budget. It reaches the exact ethically minded segment, communicates the $2.50 premium and the 58% labour-practices concern, and costs far less than television, which is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted. Search alone is rejected because it cannot build the awareness a new range needs.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited description of promotional methods with minimal reference to JRC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two methods applied to JRC's boutique and online business.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three methods with a justified recommendation that rejects television and explains the limits of search advertising.

questions.question_text: JRC's labour turnover is rising and garment return rates have increased. Explain two benefits for JRC of using democratic leadership to improve motivation in its boutiques.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership gives the 36 staff a voice in how boutique displays and the new stock-control tablets are used, raising job satisfaction and commitment. That directly tackles rising labour turnover and the cost of retraining, while engaged staff check garments more carefully, helping reduce the 4.3% returns rate.

Point 2: Consulting employees generates practical ideas from those handling the 11,400 garments sold each quarter, so sizing or quality faults behind returns are spotted early. In a hierarchical structure democratic consultation softens top-down decisions, making the $820 college courses and on-the-job training more effective and protecting the $760,000 hub investment.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit of democratic leadership identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to JRC's turnover, returns, structure and training.

questions.question_text: JRC must train 11 staff to use the new stock-control tablets. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the local college. Which should JRC choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Coaching in each boutique is specific to JRC's tablets and customer service, costs no fees, and keeps the 11 staff selling the 11,400 garments handled last quarter. It helps reduce the 4.3% returns rate through immediate correction. Drawbacks are that the coach's selling time falls, bad habits can spread, and there is no external certificate.

Off-the-job training: College courses at $820 per employee cost $9,020 for the 11 staff, a small part of the $760,000 investment. They provide structured skills and a recognised certificate, valuable for a cooperative accountable to members. However, staff are away from the boutiques, which may lengthen the 6.4-day replenishment time, and generic content may not match JRC's tablets, requiring on-site follow-up.

Decision: JRC should choose on-the-job training first, with short college updates later. It is cheaper, tablet-specific and avoids losing selling time while labour turnover is rising and returns remain a concern. Full off-the-job training is rejected because $9,020 and the absence of 11 staff would disrupt boutique service during the hub rollout, and democratic leadership supports peer coaching in the shops.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to JRC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analysis of benefits and drawbacks of both methods in JRC's context with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods with a justified decision covering cost, disruption, returns and tablet relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how JRC's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $266,000 ÷ ($34 − $20) = $266,000 ÷ $14 = 19,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 19,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $34 − $20 = $14.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $14.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways JRC's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare break-even output of 19,000 units with output of 48,000 units to show a margin of safety of 29,000 units, confirming the new hub can operate without losses.
2. Use the $2.50 premium that 66% of shoppers accept to model contribution rising from $14.00 toward $16.50, supporting the ethical sourcing decision.
3. Set volumes that cover $266,000 fixed costs and $460,000 loan repayments, checking the 48,000-unit plan can service debt.
4. Track unit cost ($266,000 ÷ 48,000 + $20 = $25.54) each quarter to benchmark the hub and detect waste behind the 4.3% returns rate.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 19,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $14.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety against 48,000-unit output; modelling the $2.50 ethical premium; loan-service volume targets; and unit-cost benchmarking at $25.54 to monitor returns.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for the accurate numerical answer in each of (i) and (ii); 1 mark per valid applied use in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate JRC's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has JRC's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.79 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 2.02 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.61 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.91 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $132,000 + $40,000 + $28,000 = $200,000; 2025 current assets = $118,000 + $52,000 + $44,000 = $214,000. For 2024, $200,000 ÷ $112,000 = 1.79; for 2025, $214,000 ÷ $106,000 = 2.02. Excluding stock: 2024 ($200,000 − $132,000) ÷ $112,000 = $68,000 ÷ $112,000 = 0.61; 2025 ($214,000 − $118,000) ÷ $106,000 = $96,000 ÷ $106,000 = 0.91.

Evaluation: Liquidity has clearly strengthened. Coverage of short-term obligations rose from 1.79 to 2.02 because current liabilities fell from $112,000 to $106,000 while assets rose. More importantly, the stock-excluding measure improved from 0.61 to 0.91, so JRC is far less dependent on selling inventory to meet debts, which is valuable while it services a $460,000 loan and spends $760,000 on a hub. Cash rose from $28,000 to $44,000 and inventories fell from $132,000 to $118,000. The concern is receivables rising from $40,000 to $52,000, tying up cash; slow payment could weaken the gain.

Conclusion: JRC's financial position has improved. Both measures rose and the stock-excluding measure confirms the improvement is not driven by inventory alone. Tighter credit control on the higher receivables would help, but the cooperative can fund the hub from a stronger liquidity base.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates both ratios for both years with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables, cash and liabilities and a justified conclusion.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for JRC of sourcing fair-trade clothing for its ethical fashion range.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Fair-trade sourcing matches the 66% of 410 shoppers who would pay up to $2.50 more and the 58% who check labour practices, protecting the $14.00 contribution per unit as fabric and import costs rise 10.4%. It strengthens the brand behind the $760,000 distribution hub.

Disadvantage: Fair-trade certified fabric usually costs more than standard cloth, raising the $20 variable cost per unit unless the full $2.50 premium is accepted. Any supply delay would lengthen the 6.4-day replenishment time and risk complaints, while the 4.3% returns rate still needs attention at the new hub.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to JRC's survey data, costs and expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.25%, the 5.8% minimum wage increase and the 10.4% rise in fabric and import costs will affect JRC. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.5% to 5.25%): If JRC's $460,000 ten-year bank loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost rises by 0.75% of $460,000 = $3,450 a year (0.0075 × $460,000). That is modest beside fixed costs of $266,000, and if the loan is fixed-rate there is no direct cost. Higher rates may slow ethical-fashion spending and raise future borrowing costs, but JRC can manage this by fixing the rate.

Minimum wage increase (5.8%, to $14.18 an hour): With a workforce of 36, higher hourly pay increases JRC's wage bill and cannot be avoided. The insert states no hours worked or individual wages, so an annual total cannot be invented; the defensible benchmark is productivity of 48,000 ÷ 36 = 1,333.3 units per worker. If productivity holds, the rise is absorbable; if it falls, the $14.00 contribution per unit is eroded.

Fabric and import inflation (10.4%): The $20 variable cost per unit is exposed, but the insert does not decompose it, so only an illustrative bound is honest: if the whole variable cost rose 10.4%, that adds 10.4% × $20 = $2.08 per unit, about $99,800 a year at 48,000 units. The $2.50 premium 66% of shoppers accept can recover part of this.

Conclusion: The 10.4% rise in fabric and import costs has the greatest impact. It applies to every garment, directly threatens the $14.00 contribution that justifies the $760,000 hub, and is only partly offset by higher prices; the interest effect is modest and the wage effect depends on hours not given in the insert.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to JRC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on JRC's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three changes in JRC's context with a justified greatest-impact judgement that avoids invented figures.
